idiom_name: data class + compiler-generated copy(...) with named overrides
implementation_notes: For a data class the compiler generates a copy() whose parameters default to the current property values, so 'take this configured instance and change two fields' is an ordinary call: template.copy(region = "EU"). It is a shallow copy - properties that reference mutable objects are shared, exactly as the language reference warns - so a deep copy is written as an explicit body that recreates nested values (or calls their copy()). For non-data classes write a copy constructor or your own fun copy(); the JVM Cloneable/clone() route is available but keeps the shallow-copy semantics, the unchecked cast and CloneNotSupportedException, so it is rarely idiomatic in Kotlin.
code_sketch:
data class Campaign(
    val code: String,
    val percent: Int,
    val region: String = "global",
)

val base = Campaign("BF24", 20)
val eu = base.copy(region = "EU", percent = 22)   // shallow clone + overrides
pitfalls: copy() is shallow: copy(roles = roles) keeps the same MutableList, so mutating it through the copy changes the original (kotlinlang documents this explicitly).
copy() only covers primary-constructor properties; state declared in the class body is not copied and can leave the clone inconsistent.
Relying on JVM clone() bypasses constructors and returns Any: prefer copy()/copy constructors to keep types and invariants.
